issue_context.title: NETCONF connections/plugins require rework to support collections
issue_context.body:
##### SUMMARY
Ansible platform contains some hard coded behaviour that blocks making NETCONF plugins pluggable using Collections (Galaxy).

Detailed issues:
1. NETCONF connection plugin contains a dictionary called `NETWORK_OS_DEVICE_PARAM_MAP` that translates from `ansible_network_os` to name of the ncclient device_handler. If adding a new networking OS using collections, it is rather unclear how this list can be extended. In the particular case, I am using network OS `nokia.sros.sros` - which obviously is not a known device-handler supported by ncclient.
As the number of native device handlers supported by ncclient is very limited, the alternative option would be just to provide mappings to known device-handlers - while for all other platforms the ncclient "default" device handler would be used.
Another alternative could be, to use just the strip the collection name and namespace - so in the case above, it would translate to just "sros". However, the vendor/contributor must ensure that ncclient has a device handler with that name - which in case of "sros" would not be the case today (aka default works fine).

2. The method `get_device_info` returns a dictionary that has the key `network_os`. It is rather unclear, if this value is related to the `ansible_network_os` that is defined in the host inventory. In this particular case, it is assumed to return `sros` or `nokia.sros.sros`?

3. The method `guess_network_os` returns the guessed network OS. Same as (2), is there any expectation, that it returns simply `sros` or the full string `nokia.sros.sros`.

General comments about device family auto discovery:
- The implementation of `ansible_network_os = auto` is rather inefficient. For every known vendor Ansible connects via NETCONF and disconnects. It would be rather preferred, to simply connect via NETCONF once and keep the connection open. The server capabilities exchanged could be passed to the different plugins, to do an initial assessment based on the existence of certain capability values. The plugin might run a few more additional netconf-get requests, if the hello exchange does not contain enough information to take a decision.
- Device auto-negotiation should have a priority/preference values. That way, people could steer the order of detection to optimise performance but also to provide a more predictable result. In the particular case, there is Ansible built-in support for NETCONF on Nokia SROS devices. However, to remove vendor specific code from Ansible core, we've started to move the corresponding code to the collection "nokia.sros.sros". How can a developer or operator influence Ansible, so the auto-detection method from the collection is preferred against the built-on method (which likely will become deprecated with the next Ansible release)?
- It's rather unclear, how auto-discovery works across different protocols. Let's say, we want to do automation against Nokia SROS devices, while setting the `ansible_network_os` to `auto`. In that case, the expectation would be, that the network_os detection is only executed once - but can be used for various connection types: NETCONF, CLI, ....

##### ISSUE TYPE
- Bug Report

##### COMPONENT NAME
lib/ansible/plugins/connection/netconf.py

##### ANSIBLE VERSION
```
ansible 2.9.2
  config file = None
  configured module search path = ['/Users/wiso/.ansible/plugins/modules', '/usr/share/ansible/plugins/modules']
  ansible python module location = /usr/local/lib/python3.7/site-packages/ansible
  executable location = /usr/local/bin/unusable
  python version = 3.7.5 (default, Nov  1 2019, 02:16:32) [Clang 11.0.0 (clang-1100.0.33.8)]
```

##### STEPS TO REPRODUCE
Check with collection `nokia.sros`

@ganeshrn, please have a look into the above. It would be good to understand how this is supposed to work. If you have a collection that contains a NETCONF plugin this would be great thing to share - however, I've checked on Galaxy and did not found any.
You might use the code from collection `nokia.sros.sros` as a reference. Please let me know, if this is something that would be fixed in a Ansible 2.9.x maintenance release, or if we need to wait until Ansible 2.10.

@wisotzky 
> 1) NETCONF connection plugin contains a dictionary called NETWORK_OS_DEVICE_PARAM_MAP that translates from ansible_network_os to name of the ncclient device_handler. If adding a new networking OS using collections, it is rather unclear how this list can be extended. In the particular case, I am using network OS nokia.sros.sros - which obviously is not a known device-handler supported by ncclient.
As the number of native device handlers supported by ncclient is very limited, the alternative option would be just to provide mappings to known device-handlers - while for all other platforms the ncclient "default" device handler would be used.
Another alternative could be, to use just the strip the collection name and namespace - so in the case above, it would translate to just "sros". However, the vendor/contributor must ensure that ncclient has a device handler with that name - which in case of "sros" would not be the case today (aka default works fine).

The fix in PR https://github.com/ansible/ansible/pull/65718 makes netconf plugins as configurable. So the information about ncclient device handler will reside in the plugin itself.
which will be pulled in the netconf connection plugin. The advantage of this approach is not having a hardcoded mapping between ansible_network_os and ncclient device handler. The platform owner has full control to set the correct value of the device handler in the platform-specific netconf plugin.


> 2) The method get_device_info returns a dictionary that has the key network_os. It is rather unclear, if this value is related to the ansible_network_os that is defined in the host inventory. In this particular case, it is assumed to return sros or nokia.sros.sros?


After the netconf plugin is moved into the collection it make sense to return the fully qualified network os name. That is `nokia.sros.sros` in your case.


> 3) The method guess_network_os returns the guessed network OS. Same as (2), is there any expectation, that it returns simply sros or the full string nokia.sros.sros.

The `guess_network_os` current logic won't work for netconf plugins in the collection. I am checking with other stakeholders if it is possible to achieve the functionality when plugins are moved to their respective collections. 

>  The implementation of ansible_network_os = auto is rather inefficient. For every known vendor Ansible connects via NETCONF and disconnects. It would be rather preferred, to simply connect via NETCONF once and keep the connection open. The server capabilities exchanged could be passed to the different plugins, to do an initial assessment based on the existence of certain capability values. 

The connection created in `guess_network_os` needs to close as after the value of the device handler is identified the connection needs to be recreated passing the device handler value to the ncclient manager object at the time of connection initialization. ncclient does not support loading on device handler specific functions after the manager object is created.

>  The plugin might run a few more additional netconf-get requests, if the hello exchange does not contain enough information to take a decision.


If the hello capability exchange doesn't get the information about the network os, in that case, the platform plugin can implement the logic to run additional RPC's to retrieve the os name.


>  Device auto-negotiation should have a priority/preference values. That way, people could steer the order of detection to optimise performance but also to provide a more predictable result. In the particular case, there is Ansible built-in support for NETCONF on Nokia SROS devices. However, to remove vendor specific code from Ansible core, we've started to move the corresponding code to the collection "nokia.sros.sros". How can a developer or operator influence Ansible, so the auto-detection method from the collection is preferred against the built-on method (which likely will become deprecated with the next Ansible release)?

If we are able to support this feature in collections the priority/preference can be controlled by the sequence in which the collections are mentioned under the `collections` keyword for the given play.eg:
```
  collections:
  - network.common
  - nokia.sros
  - cisco.iosxr
  - juniper.junos
```

> It's rather unclear, how auto-discovery works across different protocols. Let's say, we want to do automation against Nokia SROS devices, while setting the ansible_network_os to auto. In that case, the expectation would be, that the network_os detection is only executed once - but can be used for various connection types: NETCONF, CLI, 

The persistent connection depends on the value of connection type so the information about the network os identified with netconf connection type cannot be passed on to a process (task) that runs with a different connection type say network_cli.
To achieve sharing of the detected os name information across connection probably the name of the network os identified and capabilities can be returned in say `netconf_get` module result.
This information can be used to set the network os value within the play that can be used by other tasks running with the different connection types within a playbook/roles.
@ganeshrn, thanks for the fast response. From the code it looks that this would be planned to be shipped as part of Ansible 2.10... What is the method to be used until 2.10 will be released?

@wisotzky I will check with the 2.9 release manager if we can backport this PR to stable-2.9 branch. If the PR is backported it will be available in the 2.9 minor release and can be used with Ansible 2.9.X version itself.
@ganeshrn, thx for putting effort in cross-checking potential of backporting this!
@ganeshrn, I've updated the Nokia SR OS collection `nokia.sros` to reflect those changed made. However, still need to setup my system accordingly to run some tests on this.

@wisotzky Did you get a chance to test the PR? If it works I will merge it and raise a 2.9 backport PR. 

Also after internal discussion, we concluded that `ansible_network_os=auto` feature will be deprecated and removed in 2.10. The netconf auto-discovery feature won't be supported in collections. Since in most of the case the network os value is already known to enable netconf on the device which is a prerequisite before using any of the netconf related features.

@ganeshrn, @trishnaguha 

Might be good if you could have another look into my terminal plugins for `nokia.sros.md` and `nokia.sros.classic`. I've added a check if the correct configuration mode is active. If not, I was about to issue a warning. 

For this, I've added the following code snippets:
```python
from ansible.utils.display import Display
from ansible.module_utils._text import to_text
```

```python
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super(TerminalModule, self).__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.display = Display()
```

```python
            reply = self._exec_cli_command(b'/show system information')
            data = to_text(reply, errors='surrogate_or_strict').strip()
            match = re.search(r'Configuration Mode Oper:\s+(.+)', data)
            if not match or match.group(1) == 'classic':
                self.display.warning("Nokia SROS node is running in classic mode. Use:\n  ansible_network_os: nokia.sros.classic")
```

In my system, those warnings do not get logged to Ansible console. So it seems that `self.display.warning()` and `self.display.display()` do not work in context of a terminal (and cliconf) plugin methods. I've validated that its not an issue of the if-condition. However, adding such print statements into the constructor I am seeing the messages being displayed.

Any ideas?

In general I would like to better understand the concept for plugins to return errors or with warnings. My impression so far is, that there is no concept to return with warnings - so the workaround is using Display().warning(...) - which did not worked in my case. For errors it seems the way to go is raising exceptions. The unfortunate part is that exceptions get logged at Ansible console with full stack trace - while regular operators would like to see is the actual error message.

Likely there is work required to improve generic networking modules like `cli_command` and `cli_config` to have proper handling for alarms and warnings implemented.

@ganeshrn, @trishnaguha

One more question:
I've added a new module `device_info` into our `nokia.sros` collection. This is basically calling the `get_device_info()` method from the Cliconf module to extract some information. This was done to avoid implementing a full blown facts or resource module for Nokia SR OS - as we would claim that NETCONF by providing structured data is the much better approach than building a CLI wrapper overlay.

However, is there a good resource that clarifies the past, current and future implementation for basic network node inventory (aka hostname, release/version, ...)? From my knowledge currently the `gather_facts` flag triggers the new resource modules - while this seems to be an overkill for our purposes. Indeed, it would be much better if any cliconf and netconf plugin would implement a basic `get_facts_brief` method, that returns some basic network device inventory information.

Hi @ganeshrn 

> @wisotzky Did you get a chance to test the PR? If it works I will merge it and raise a 2.9 backport PR.

I've validated your change with collection `nokia.sros` using network OS `nokia.sros.md`. Works like charm. I would propose to merge the change and back port to Ansible 2.9.

@ganeshrn, @trishnaguha 

Looking into the new NETCONF connection/plugin code, there seems to be a way to define options per plugin:
```YAML
options:
  ncclient_device_handler:
    type: str
    default: default
```
Just wondering, if such options are accessible from inside the plugin (answer seems to be yes) and if those options can be overwritten (global, playbook, task level). More specifically I was wondering about the generic `cli_config` Ansible module. For Nokia SR OS it would be useful to control the usage of the nodal rollback feature. If rollback is used, resulting behaviour would be `rollback-on-error` if not it would result in `stop-on-error`.

I was just wondering, if plugin `options` are a reasonable method to control the plugin behaviour as in the particular case `cli_config` does not provide enough control. Alternative would be, to create another `network-os` called `nokia.sros.basic` in addition to the existing `nokia.sros.classic` and `nokia.sros.md` network-os values.

@wisotzky Yes, you can control the plugin options as global, playbook and task level. For example, refer https://github.com/ansible/ansible/blob/devel/lib/ansible/plugins/connection/network_cli.py#L148

@wisotzky Yes by design the logs are queued and displayed at the end of the task run. Reopening the issue to use it to track the netconf auto depreciation changes.
Raised 2.9 backport PR https://github.com/ansible/ansible/pull/65991

> @wisotzky Yes by design the logs are queued and displayed at the end of the task run. If the user is expected to use `ansible_network_os: nokia.sros.classic` why not raise an `AnsibleError` exception in the terminal plugin itself instead of providing a warning?

Main reason we wanted to avoid `AnsibleError` is to achieve idempotency for playbooks that do initial node commissioning (day0 operation): If a Nokia SROS node becomes online the first time, it runs in classic mode. A configuration change is required to enable MD mode, while after the change the CLI user must re-login. The way those SROS plugins are written, one can run `show` commands and determine the current mode (model-driven versus classic) without issuing errors. The mode is only enforced using `AnsibleError` for configuration changes using the Ansible `cli_config` module.

However, adding a warning makes absolutely sense to us, because trouble-shooting errors due to the use of the wrong plugin is sometimes not straight forward - especially as errors always contain the full stack trace. Also there are differences for other CLI commands (not just configuration) so people might wonder, why a certain command is sometimes not working (aka generating a CLI error).

The only alternative would be, to add the `ignore_errors: yes` setting into the corresponding task. However, this looks ugly and should be avoided. For us, it looks cleaner to check the mode first and skip tasks if the node already run in model-driven mode.
 
> You can provide the node reference in the message itself by referring to `self._connection.get_option('host')`

@ganeshrn, I've added the `get_option('host')` in version 1.4.2 of the `nokia.sros` collection.
